title: Anthropic Tool Use
summary: Anthropic tool use is how Claude actually calls tools: you declare tools with a name, description, and input JSON Schema; Claude replies with a tool_use content block instead of prose; your code runs the function and returns a tool_result block; and you loop until Claude stops requesting tools. You can force or restrict which tool Claude picks with tool_choice, and the whole exchange is just the general reason-act-observe agent loop expressed in Claude's message format — the same shape every provider uses under different names.

subtopics.title: Declaring a tool with an input_schema
subtopics.explanation: You pass Claude a list of tools, each with a name, a natural-language description, and an input_schema that is a JSON Schema describing the arguments. The description is prompt text the model reads to decide when to use the tool, and the schema constrains the arguments it emits. Getting the description and schema right is what makes Claude call the tool at the correct moment with well-formed inputs, which is the whole foundation of tool use.

subtopics.title: Claude replies with a tool_use block
subtopics.explanation: When Claude decides to use a tool, it does not run it — it returns an assistant message whose stop_reason is 'tool_use' and whose content contains a tool_use block with a unique id, the tool name, and an input dict already matching your schema. Your code inspects the content blocks and dispatches on the name. Recognizing that a tool_use block is a request (not an execution) is the single idea that makes the rest of the flow make sense.
subtopics.example:
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris?"}],
)

# find the tool_use block in the response content
for block in resp.content:
    if block.type == "tool_use":
        print(block.id)     # 'toolu_01A...' unique call id
        print(block.name)   # 'get_weather'
        print(block.input)  # {'city': 'Paris'} -- already schema-shaped
# stop_reason == 'tool_use' means Claude wants a result back

subtopics.title: Returning a tool_result
subtopics.explanation: You run the requested function, then send a new user-role message containing a tool_result block that references the original tool_use_id and carries the output. Claude reads that observation and continues. The tool_use_id linkage is what pairs a result with the exact call that asked for it, which is essential once Claude issues several tool calls at once.

subtopics.title: Forcing or restricting tool choice
subtopics.explanation: By default tool_choice is 'auto' — Claude decides whether to call a tool or just answer. You can set it to 'any' to force it to call some tool, to {'type': 'tool', 'name': ...} to force one specific tool, or 'none' to forbid tools for that turn. Forcing choice is how you guarantee structured extraction or route a step deterministically, trading a little of the model's judgment for control you can rely on.
subtopics.example:
# force Claude to call exactly this tool (e.g. for extraction)
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[extract_fields_tool],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_fields"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": doc_text}],
)
# 'auto' -> Claude decides; 'any' -> must use some tool;
# 'none' -> no tools this turn. Here it MUST call extract_fields.

subtopics.title: It maps onto the general agent loop
subtopics.explanation: Strip the provider names and this is exactly reason -> act -> observe: Claude reasons and emits a tool_use (act request), your code runs the tool and returns a tool_result (observe), and you loop while stop_reason is 'tool_use'. OpenAI calls the same pieces tool_calls and role='tool' messages; the shape is identical. Seeing tool use as one concrete instance of the universal loop lets you port an agent across providers with only glue-code changes.
subtopics.example:
def run_agent(client, tools, impls, user_msg):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
    while True:
        resp = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=1024,
            tools=tools, messages=messages,
        )
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":   # done reasoning
            return resp.content[0].text
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
        results = []
        for b in resp.content:
            if b.type == "tool_use":
                out = impls[b.name](**b.input)   # act
                results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                                "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": out})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})  # observe

foundations.overview: Anthropic's tool use is the concrete mechanism behind an agent loop on Claude. You supply a tools list where each tool has a name, description, and input_schema (a JSON Schema). When Claude wants to act, it returns an assistant message with stop_reason 'tool_use' and one or more tool_use content blocks, each carrying a unique id, the tool name, and an input object already shaped to your schema. Claude never executes anything — your code dispatches on the name, runs the function, and returns the output as a tool_result block (linked by tool_use_id) in a new user-role message. You repeat this exchange until stop_reason is no longer 'tool_use'. The tool_choice parameter lets you leave the decision to Claude ('auto'), force some tool ('any'), pin one specific tool, or forbid tools ('none'). Because the same reason-act-observe structure appears in every provider's API (OpenAI's tool_calls plus role='tool' messages are the direct analog), understanding this one flow transfers everywhere.
foundations.formalDefinition: Anthropic tool use is a Messages API protocol in which the client declares tools as {name, description, input_schema}, the model may respond with tool_use content blocks (id, name, input) and stop_reason='tool_use', and the client replies with tool_result blocks referencing each tool_use_id; iteration continues until the model returns a non-tool_use stop_reason. tool_choice ('auto' | 'any' | {'type':'tool','name':...} | 'none') controls whether and which tool the model must call.
foundations.whyItMatters: Tool use is the single API surface that turns Claude from a text generator into an agent that can query systems and take actions. Every higher-level capability — MCP servers, RAG retrieval, multi-tool orchestration — is built on this request/observe exchange, so mastering the tool_use / tool_result flow is prerequisite to everything that follows.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of Claude as a colleague on a phone line who can only talk. When they need data they say 'please run get_weather for Paris, tag this request #A1'; you hang up, run it yourself, call back and say 'result for #A1: 18C rain'. The tool_use block is their request, the tool_result is your callback, and the id is the ticket number that keeps parallel requests straight.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Claude-powered coding assistants that read files and run tests, support agents that look up orders, data agents that run SQL, and extraction pipelines that force a single tool call to return typed fields — all use this exact tool_use / tool_result loop, often wrapped by an SDK or by MCP.
foundations.performanceImpact: Each loop iteration is a full model round-trip, so latency scales with tool-call depth; letting Claude request several tools in one assistant turn (parallel tool use) and returning all their results together cuts the number of round-trips versus forcing one tool per turn.
commonUseCases: Wiring Claude to real APIs (search, DB, calendar)
Forcing a single tool call for typed extraction
Multi-step agents that loop on stop_reason='tool_use'
Porting an existing agent between Claude and other providers

commonMisconceptions.myth: Claude runs the tool and gives you the answer.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Claude only emits a tool_use request with arguments. Your code runs the function and must send the output back as a tool_result before Claude can use it.
'auto' lets Claude answer without any tool; 'any' forces it to call some tool. Use 'any' or a named tool when you require a structured tool call every time.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Tool use on Claude is fundamentally different from other providers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's the same reason-act-observe loop; only the field names differ (tool_use/tool_result vs OpenAI's tool_calls/role='tool'). The design ports directly.

codeLab.title: Implement the tool-use loop driver
codeLab.instructions: Implement run_tool_loop(client, tools, impls, user_msg) that drives an Anthropic-style tool-use conversation. It must: (1) start messages with the user message; (2) call client.messages.create(model='claude-sonnet-4-5', max_tokens=1024, tools=tools, messages=messages) each iteration; (3) if resp.stop_reason != 'tool_use', return the text of the first content block; (4) otherwise append the assistant turn ({'role':'assistant','content':resp.content}), run each tool_use block via impls[name](**input), collect a tool_result block for each (with the matching tool_use_id), append them as one user message ({'role':'user','content':results}), and loop. Cap the loop at 10 iterations, raising RuntimeError if it never finishes. The provided fake client and tools let the harness verify your loop.

starter.code:
def run_tool_loop(client, tools, impls, user_msg):
    # TODO: drive the tool_use / tool_result loop.
    # - loop while stop_reason == 'tool_use'
    # - run impls[name](**input) for each tool_use block
    # - return the text once Claude stops requesting tools
    # - cap at 10 iterations, else raise RuntimeError
    ...

solution.code:
def run_tool_loop(client, tools, impls, user_msg):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}]
    for _ in range(10):                       # hard iteration cap
        resp = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=1024,
            tools=tools, messages=messages,
        )
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":    # Claude is done acting
            return resp.content[0].text
        # record Claude's tool requests before answering them
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
        results = []
        for b in resp.content:
            if getattr(b, "type", None) == "tool_use":
                out = impls[b.name](**b.input)          # act (our code runs it)
                results.append({
                    "type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": b.id,               # link result to the call
                    "content": out,
                })
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})  # observe
    raise RuntimeError("tool loop did not converge in 10 iterations")

hints: Loop while resp.stop_reason == 'tool_use'; return resp.content[0].text once it is anything else (e.g. 'end_turn').
Append the assistant turn ({'role':'assistant','content':resp.content}) BEFORE the tool_result message, or Claude loses the context of its own request.
Each tool_result must carry tool_use_id equal to the id of the tool_use block that requested it, and all results go in one user message.

theory.question: Walk through the Anthropic tool_use / tool_result message flow.
theory.directAnswer: You send a tools list (each with name, description, input_schema). Claude may respond with stop_reason 'tool_use' and tool_use content blocks (id, name, input). Your code runs each tool and replies with a user message of tool_result blocks referencing the matching tool_use_id. You loop until stop_reason is no longer 'tool_use', at which point Claude returns its final text.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A request/observe protocol on the Messages API where the model asks for tool calls and the client supplies results, iterating to completion.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The model can reason and choose arguments but cannot touch your systems; the protocol cleanly separates the model's decision from your code's execution while keeping both in one conversation.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Declare tools with JSON Schemas; on stop_reason 'tool_use' dispatch on block.name, run the function, append the assistant turn plus tool_result blocks linked by tool_use_id, and re-call the API until a non-tool_use stop_reason returns the answer.

theory.whyImportant: It is the base layer every Claude agent, MCP integration, and orchestration pattern is built on, so getting the loop and the id linkage right is fundamental.
theory.realWorldExample: A support agent asks Claude a question, Claude requests get_order(id='A-1'), the code runs it and returns the order as a tool_result, and Claude then composes a reply citing the order status.

followUps.question: Why does each tool_result carry a tool_use_id?
followUps.answer: So a result is paired with the exact call that requested it, which is required when Claude issues several tool calls in one turn (parallel tool use).

followUps.question: What signals the loop is done?
followUps.answer: stop_reason changes from 'tool_use' to something like 'end_turn', meaning Claude has enough information and returned final text.

theory.question: What does tool_choice control, and when would you use 'any' or a named tool instead of 'auto'?
theory.directAnswer: tool_choice governs whether and which tool Claude must call: 'auto' lets Claude decide (answer or call), 'any' forces it to call some tool, {'type':'tool','name':X} forces one specific tool, and 'none' forbids tools. Use 'any' or a named tool when you require a structured tool call every time — for example forcing an extraction tool so you always get typed arguments rather than prose.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A request parameter constraining the model's tool-calling decision for a turn.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Sometimes you want the model's judgment (auto) and sometimes you need a guaranteed, deterministic tool call for structured output or fixed routing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The API biases or hard-constrains generation so the model must emit a tool_use block matching the allowed tool(s); 'none' suppresses tool blocks entirely for that turn.

theory.whyImportant: It trades a slice of model autonomy for control, which is essential for reliable extraction and for routing steps that must always call a particular tool.
theory.realWorldExample: A document pipeline sets tool_choice to the extract_fields tool so every call returns {invoice_no, total, date} as arguments, never a chatty paragraph.

followUps.question: What's a downside of forcing 'any' everywhere?
followUps.answer: You lose Claude's ability to just answer when no tool is needed, which can force awkward or wasteful tool calls; scope forcing to turns that truly need it.

followUps.question: Does 'auto' guarantee a tool is never called?
followUps.answer: No — 'auto' means Claude may or may not call a tool; use 'none' to actually forbid tool use for that turn.

scenario.question: Your Claude agent occasionally loops forever re-calling the same tool and other times crashes with a 'tool_use ids must have corresponding tool_result' API error. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Both symptoms come from a malformed message history. Fix the history contract: always append the assistant turn (resp.content) before the tool_result message, return exactly one tool_result per tool_use id every turn, and add a hard iteration cap plus a check that impls covers every tool name. Log stop_reason and the ids per turn to confirm each tool_use is answered.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A protocol-conformance and termination bug in the tool-use loop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The API requires every tool_use block to be answered by a tool_result with the same id in the next user message; skipping the assistant turn, dropping an id, or never terminating breaks that contract.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Trace one failing conversation: if the assistant tool_use turn is missing you get the API error; if a tool raises and you skip its result you get a missing-id error; if you never check stop_reason or cap iterations you get infinite re-calls. Restore the append-assistant-then-all-results ordering, wrap each tool in try/except returning an error tool_result, and cap the loop.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the candidate understands the exact message-ordering and id-pairing contract that makes tool use work, plus the safety cap every agent loop needs.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team found one tool raised on bad input; they had skipped appending its tool_result, so the next request had an unanswered tool_use id and 500'd. Returning an error string as the tool_result fixed both the crash and the re-loop.

followUps.question: How should a tool exception be surfaced to Claude?
followUps.answer: Return a tool_result with is_error true and a short error message so Claude can adapt, rather than dropping the result and breaking the id pairing.

followUps.question: Why add an iteration cap even after fixing the history?
followUps.answer: A model can still choose to keep calling tools; a hard cap bounds cost and latency and turns a stuck loop into a handled failure.

coding.question: Write a dispatcher that, given a response's content blocks and an impls dict, runs every tool_use block and returns the list of tool_result blocks, capturing tool exceptions as error results.
coding.thoughtProcess: I iterate the content blocks, act only on type 'tool_use', and look up the implementation by name. I run it inside try/except so a failing tool becomes a tool_result with is_error true instead of breaking the id pairing. Each result echoes the block's id via tool_use_id so Claude can match it, and I return the full list to append as one user message.
lineByLine: Skip any content block that is not a tool_use so text blocks are ignored.
Look up the implementation by block.name; an unknown tool raises KeyError, handled below.
Call the function with **b.input, the schema-shaped arguments Claude produced.
On success, emit a tool_result linked by tool_use_id with the stringified output.
On any exception, emit a tool_result with is_error True so Claude sees the failure and can adapt instead of the loop breaking on a missing id.
The __main__ block shows one successful add and one failing tool both producing valid result blocks.
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) in the number of content blocks, times the cost of each tool call.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the list of result blocks returned.

followUps.question: Why stringify tool output?
followUps.answer: tool_result content is text (or content blocks); non-string outputs must be serialized so Claude can read them, e.g. json.dumps for structured data.

followUps.question: How does this enable parallel tool use?
followUps.answer: It handles many tool_use blocks from one assistant turn and returns all their results together, so Claude can request several tools at once and get every answer in a single follow-up.

keyTakeaways: Declare tools as {name, description, input_schema}; the description tells Claude when to call and the schema shapes the arguments.
Claude never runs tools — a tool_use block (id, name, input) with stop_reason 'tool_use' is a request your code must execute.
Return each result as a tool_result block linked by tool_use_id in a user message, and loop while stop_reason stays 'tool_use'.
tool_choice controls calling: 'auto' (decide), 'any' (must call some tool), a named tool (must call that one), 'none' (forbid) — force it for guaranteed structured calls.
This is the general reason-act-observe loop in Claude's format; OpenAI's tool_calls/role='tool' is the same shape, so the design ports across providers.
